record.paper_title: Multiparty Quantum Key Agreement: Architectures, State-of-the-art, and Open Problems
record.original_question: Can multiparty quantum key agreement methods be extended to emerging multiparty cryptographic applications—especially (t,n)-threshold schemes, quantum private comparison, and hybrid classical–quantum ledgers—so that quantum mechanics, fairness, and collusion resistance provide concrete security advantages for key recovery, private comparison, authentication, consensus, or transaction validity?

evidence.quote: Within the realm of cryptography, MQKA keys can be effectively utilized in (t,n)-threshold schemes, where t shares are required for key recovery. This raises the intriguing question of whether quantum mechanics can enhance the security of these threshold schemes.

MQKA techniques extend beyond key agreement into more generalized multiparty quantum protocols, such as quantum private comparison. The essential principles of fairness and collusion resistance inherent in MQKA directly apply to these protocols, enhancing their security and functionality.
Another promising application area is the integration of MQKA with blockchain technology to create hybrid classical-quantum ledgers.
The implementation of fairness-aware MQKA is crucial for ensuring the validity of distributed quantum ledger systems, where equitable participation and trust among users are paramount.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A multiparty quantum key agreement (MQKA) protocol is a protocol in which n mutually distrustful parties P_1,...,P_n jointly establish a common secret key K such that (i) every party contributes equally to K (fairness), (ii) no proper subset of parties can predetermine or bias K (collusion resistance), and (iii) security against external eavesdroppers is guaranteed by the laws of quantum mechanics.

Investigate whether the design principles and security guarantees of MQKA can be lifted to the following three multiparty cryptographic primitives, and in each case either construct a protocol meeting the stated security goals or prove an impossibility result:

1. (t,n)-threshold key schemes. Design an MQKA-based protocol that produces shares s_1,...,s_n of a key K such that any t shares reconstruct K while any t-1 shares reveal no information about K, with security (against both outside adversaries and coalitions of up to t-1 dishonest parties) reducible to quantum-mechanical assumptions rather than computational ones, and quantify the advantage over classical (t,n)-threshold secret sharing.

2. Quantum private comparison (QPC). Using MQKA-style fairness and collusion resistance, construct a protocol allowing n parties holding private inputs x_1,...,x_n to compute a comparison predicate (e.g. equality of all x_i) while revealing nothing else about the inputs, even under arbitrary collusions of up to n-1 participants and an untrusted assistant, and characterize the optimal trade-offs among round complexity, qubit cost, and tolerated collusion size.

3. Hybrid classical–quantum distributed ledgers. Define a distributed ledger consensus protocol in which transaction validity and authentication are derived from a fairness-aware MQKA subroutine, and prove security properties analogous to safety, liveness, and resistance to coalitions controlling a bounded fraction of parties, identifying the precise quantum-cryptographic assumption (e.g. authenticated quantum channels, no-cloning, monogamy of entanglement) that gives a provable advantage over purely classical Byzantine consensus.

The overarching question is: do quantum mechanics together with the MQKA notions of fairness and collusion resistance yield concrete, provable security advantages over the best classical schemes for key recovery, private comparison, authentication, consensus, and transaction validity in the multiparty setting?
artifact.status_search_result: The question is a broad open research direction concerning extensions of multiparty quantum key agreement to threshold schemes, quantum private comparison, and quantum-classical blockchains. While individual quantum threshold secret-sharing, QPC, and quantum blockchain protocols exist in the literature, a unified treatment establishing concrete, provable quantum security advantages over classical analogues — built from fairness- and collusion-resistant MQKA — has not been achieved, and the topic is presented as an open direction in current surveys. Status appears open.
